Moist air

Moist air is dry air with water vapor in it. Dome gives its properties through functions; there are no state lines for moist air. This page follows Help › Examples › Moist air: cooling with dehumidification.

One state

Give the pressure and two more properties.

p = 1 [atm]
w_1 = omega(moistair, p = p, T = 25 [C], phi = 0.5)
h_1 = h(moistair, p = p, T = 25 [C], phi = 0.5)
Tdp_1 = Tdp(moistair, p = p, T = 25 [C], phi = 0.5)

Dome gives w_1 = 0.009926, h_1 = 50.42 kJ/kg and Tdp_1 = 13.87 °C.

FunctionGives
omegaThe humidity ratio, kg of water vapor per kg of dry air
phiThe relative humidity, a fraction from 0 to 1
TThe temperature (the dry bulb)
TwbThe wet-bulb temperature
TdpThe dew point
pvThe partial pressure of the water vapor
h v s cpEnthalpy, volume, entropy and specific heat, each per kg of dry air
  1. Write moistair first, then p and two more named properties. Every function takes exactly these three.
  2. Besides p, give T and one of phi, omega, Twb, Tdp, pv or h.
  3. Some pairs work without T, such as omega and h. If a pair does not work, Dome's message lists the ones that do.
  4. phi is a fraction: 50 % is phi = 0.5.
  5. A variable named phi or omega is still a variable. Only a name followed by an opening parenthesis is a function.

Cooling with dehumidification

Moist air at 30 °C and 50 % relative humidity enters a dehumidifier at 280 m³/min. Water condenses on a cooling coil and leaves as saturated liquid at 10 °C, and saturated air leaves at 10 °C. The pressure is 1.013 bar.

p     = 1.013 [bar]
T_1   = 30 [C]; phi_1 = 0.5
AV_1  = 280 [m^3/min]
T_2   = 10 [C]; phi_2 = 1
omega_1 = omega(moistair, p = p, T = T_1, phi = phi_1)
omega_2 = omega(moistair, p = p, T = T_2, phi = phi_2)
h_1 = h(moistair, p = p, T = T_1, phi = phi_1)
h_2 = h(moistair, p = p, T = T_2, phi = phi_2)
v_1 = v(moistair, p = p, T = T_1, phi = phi_1)
h_3 = h(water, T = T_2, x = 0)
m_dot_a = AV_1 / v_1
m_w = omega_1 - omega_2
Q_dot = m_dot_a*(h_2 + m_w*h_3 - h_1)

Dome gives m_dot_a = 5.3201 kg/s, m_w = 0.0057114 kg of condensate per kg of dry air, and Q_dot = −184.95 kW.

  1. v is per kg of dry air, so AV_1 / v_1 is the mass flow rate of the dry air. It is the same at the inlet and the exit.
  2. The water balance gives the condensate per kg of dry air, omega_1 - omega_2.
  3. Take the condensate's h from h(water, T = T_2, x = 0). The water in moist air counts from the steam tables' reference, so the condensate's h enters the same balance.
  4. With phi_1 = 0.7, Dome gives m_w = 0.011224 and Q_dot = −256.43 kW.

The example opens this sheet with comments, a refrigerating capacity in tons and two check lines.

Mixing two streams

Two streams of moist air mix at 1 atm with no heat transfer. One has 2 kg/s of dry air at 30 °C and phi = 0.3, the other 1 kg/s at 10 °C and phi = 0.8.

p = 1 [atm]
m_a1 = 2 [kg/s]; m_a2 = 1 [kg/s]
w_1 = omega(moistair, p = p, T = 30 [C], phi = 0.3)
h_1 = h(moistair, p = p, T = 30 [C], phi = 0.3)
w_2 = omega(moistair, p = p, T = 10 [C], phi = 0.8)
h_2 = h(moistair, p = p, T = 10 [C], phi = 0.8)
m_a3 = m_a1 + m_a2
m_a3*w_3 = m_a1*w_1 + m_a2*w_2
m_a3*h_3 = m_a1*h_1 + m_a2*h_2
h_3 = h(moistair, p = p, T = T_3, omega = w_3)
phi_3 = phi(moistair, p = p, T = T_3, omega = w_3)

Dome gives T_3 = 23.35 °C and phi_3 = 0.410.

  1. Write a mass balance for the dry air, one for the water vapor, and an energy balance.
  2. p, w_3 and h_3 fix the exit. The line h_3 = h(moistair, p = p, T = T_3, omega = w_3) finds T_3.

Every stream written one way

Dry air at 30 °C mixes with moist air at 10 °C and phi = 0.8, at 1 atm. Each stream carries 1 kg/s of dry air, and the dry stream is moist air with no water.

p = 1 [atm]
m_a = 1 [kg/s]
w_1 = 0
h_1 = h(moistair, p = p, T = 30 [C], omega = 0)
w_2 = omega(moistair, p = p, T = 10 [C], phi = 0.8)
h_2 = h(moistair, p = p, T = 10 [C], phi = 0.8)
2*m_a*w_3 = m_a*w_1 + m_a*w_2
2*m_a*h_3 = m_a*h_1 + m_a*h_2
h_3 = h(moistair, p = p, T = T_3, omega = w_3)

Dome gives T_3 = 19.944 °C.

  1. Take every air stream's h from h(moistair, …), and write a dry stream with omega = 0.
  2. h(air, …) counts enthalpy from a different zero, so Dome reports an error when it meets h(moistair, …) in one balance. Written with h(air, T = 30 [C], p = p), h_1 is 303.33 kJ/kg, and the exit would be at 154.31 °C.
  3. Two other forms work when every stream is written in them. One is cp_a*(T - T_0) + omega*h(water, T = …, x = 1) with T_0 = 0 [C]; the other is h(air, …) + omega*h(water, T = …, x = 1).
  4. Written in the first form, with cp_a = 1.005 [kJ/kg/K], the mixing sheet above gives T_3 = 23.348 °C.
  5. Take the vapor's h from h(water, T = …, x = 1). h(water_ig, …) counts from 0 K, and Dome reports an error where it meets the condensate's h(water, …).
  6. One form beside another in a balance or a difference is an error, and its message names the forms that work.

On an English sheet

With English chosen in the header, this sheet gives h in Btu/lb.

p = 14.696 [psi]
T_1 = 80 [F]
w_1 = omega(moistair, p = p, T = T_1, phi = 0.5)
h_1 = h(moistair, p = p, T = T_1, phi = 0.5)

Dome gives w_1 = 0.010974 and h_1 = 31.248 Btu/lb.

  1. On an English sheet, the h of dry air is zero at 0 °F. On an SI sheet, it is zero at 0 °C.
  2. So the same state has h_1 = 54.805 kJ/kg on an SI sheet. The two differ by the h of dry air from 0 °F to 0 °C, 7.69 Btu/lb.
  3. The dry air passes through a balance unchanged, so this difference cancels from a balance whose streams are all moist air.

When Dome refuses

Each entry gives a sheet, the message Dome shows for it, and what to change.

More water vapor than the air holds

p = 1.013 [bar]
h_x = h(moistair, p = p, T = 25 [C], omega = 0.05)

h(): moist air at T = 25.00 °C and p = 1.013 bar cannot hold omega = 0.05: the most it holds is omega = 0.0201785, when it is saturated (phi = 1)

Check omega and T. A mixture of two streams that would form fog gets the same message.

Air cooled past its dew point

p = 1 [atm]
w_1 = omega(moistair, p = p, T = 30 [C], phi = 0.5)
h_2 = 40 [kJ/kg]
h_2 = h(moistair, p = p, T = T_2, omega = w_1)

no value of T_2 satisfies this equation: h(): moist air with omega = 0.0133726 at p = 1.013 bar cannot have h = 40.000 kJ/kg: the lowest is h = 52.444 kJ/kg, when it is saturated (phi = 1, T = Tdp = 18.45 °C); below the dew point some of the water vapor condenses, so the omega of the air falls

Air cooled below its dew point loses water, so omega at the exit is not w_1. Write the exit as saturated air, with phi = 1, and a water balance for the condensate, as the dehumidifier above does.

A pair outside the list

p = 1 [atm]
w = omega(moistair, p = p, phi = 0.5, Tdp = 10 [C])

omega(): moist air: phi and Tdp together are not a pair the moist-air data solve; with p, give T with any one of phi, omega, Twb, Tdp, pv or h, or one of these pairs: phi and Twb, phi and pv, phi and h, omega and Twb, omega and h, Twb and Tdp, Tdp and h

Give one of the pairs the message lists, or T with one of the properties.

A relative humidity in percent

p = 1 [atm]
w = omega(moistair, p = p, T = 25 [C], phi = 50)

omega(): moist air: phi = 50 is outside 0 to 1: relative humidity is a fraction, so 50 % is 0.5

Write phi = 0.5.

Dry air from h(air, …) beside moist air

p = 1 [atm]
m_a = 1 [kg/s]
w_1 = 0
h_1 = h(air, T = 30 [C], p = p)
w_2 = omega(moistair, p = p, T = 10 [C], phi = 0.8)
h_2 = h(moistair, p = p, T = 10 [C], phi = 0.8)
2*m_a*w_3 = m_a*w_1 + m_a*w_2
2*m_a*h_3 = m_a*h_1 + m_a*h_2
h_3 = h(moistair, p = p, T = T_3, omega = w_3)

dry air appears here from the ideal-gas model, h(air, …), and from moist air's dry air at 0 °C, h(moistair, …); use one for dry air in every term: write a dry stream as moist air with no water, h(moistair, p = …, T = …, omega = 0).

Write h_1 = h(moistair, p = p, T = 30 [C], omega = 0), as in Every stream written one way.

A state line for moist air

fluid moistair
state 1 : p = 1 [atm], T = 25 [C]

state 1: moist air is fixed by p and two other properties, so it has no state line; write it with property functions, e.g. h(moistair, p = 1 [atm], T = 25 [C], phi = 0.5)

Write each property with a function, as in One state.
